releases.legal_basis: Approval for the release of ONS Mortality data has been granted by the Office for National Statistics under the Statistics and Registration Service Act 2007 section 42(4) for the purposes of assisting the Secretary of State for Health or the Welsh Ministers in the performance of his or their functions in relation to the Health Service.

The Data Recipient agrees to process the Data only for the following purposes agreed with the HSCIC:      
Objective for processing: The project “Prognostic Factors and Outcomes for Medical Emergency Admissions” which is funded by the Welcome Trust, is investigating factors - such as week day of admission, hospital size and major services provided, and month and year of admission – that may affect outcomes following admission for various common emergency conditions in hospitals across England & Wales. The project involves utilising inpatient, mortality and GP data, the main outcome measures are mortality and readmissions, and the conditions being studied include acute MI, stroke, hip fracture, asthma and COPD. 
1. JAMIE/BRIDGE-Health: The UK is a participant in the  Joint Action on Monitoring Injuries in Europe (JAMIE) health programme.   Swansea University is the National Data Administrator for this project.   The European Injury Data Base (IDB) is maintained by European Commission DG SANCO. The European commission will only be receiving analyses results and no record-level data i.e. Case counts and risk/odds ratio’s and their respective confidence intervals.  No record-level data (pseudonymised/sensitive data) will be removed from the secured SAIL Gateway/ UK Secure eResearch Platform. Swansea University also operates the data clearing house/quality assurance function for IDB. Data from all European countries are processed through quality assurance software before being transferred to DG SANCO. From the UK perspective anonymised injury related records will be extracted from HES A&E data set and will be recoded into the JAMIE minimum data set format (five year age group, gender, occurred at home/work place/road traffic injury/other, broad category of injury e.g. soft tissue injury/fracture/sprain etc.) before being submitted to DG SANCO. No sub UK geographical details are included. This coded data set will be uploaded to a restricted access EU database (no identifiable data will be present). The data will be made available through public access and restricted access routes. The public access option will assist country comparison by Incidence Rates (IR) and therefore provides access to very limited, aggregated data presentations. The restricted access option can only be used by authorised researchers. BRIDGE-Health is the successor to the JAMIE projects and continues the activity of providing data and analysis for the EU Injury Data Base.
2. ICD10 Trauma Mortality Prediction Model: The objective is to develop an ICD10 version of the ICD9 based trauma mortality prediction model developed by Osler et al (Glance, Osler T et al. TMPM-ICD9: a trauma mortality prediction model based on ICD-9-CM codes. Annals of Surgery,2009 Jun;249(6):1032-9. doi: 10.1097/SLA.0b013e3181a38f28.). The injury severity scores produced by the regression model will be used as a risk adjustment to measure outcomes more accurately. To do this, individual row level data are required to relate individual injuries to mortality, having adjusted for age, gender, other injuries and co-morbidity. The dataset would contain no dates, no hospital identifiers, and no geographical data. Whilst there will inevitably be uniqueness within the large dataset individual privacy will be protected as the data cannot be removed or linked to any other source and only model parameters (case counts and risk/odds ratio’s and their respective confidence intervals) will be requested for removal from the SAIL Gateway/ UK Secure eResearch Platform (UK SeRP).    No raw based data will be removed from the secured SAIL Gateway/ UK Secure eResearch Platform.).  
3. UK Burden of falls project: The objective is to obtain a more accurate estimate of the burden of injuries from falls. Measuring the burden of injuries from falls, requires the calculation of Disability Adjusted Life Years (DALYs), which are a sum of Years of Life Lost (YLL) with Years Lived with Disability (YLD).  YLL are calculated by multiplying the number of deaths due to condition (e.g. falls) by the standard life expectancy at age of death.  However, in the UK (and other countries using ICD 10 mortality data) a large percentage of injury deaths are coded to a bucket code X59 (‘exposure to unspecified factor’).  Furthermore, previous analyses have demonstrated that the majority of X59 deaths appear to be attributable to hip fractures and brain injuries. In Wales the Secure Anonymised Information Linkage (www.saildatabank.com) systems' independent Information Governance Review Panel (IGRP) has approved a project to estimate this bias by linking ONS mortality data to the most recent emergency department attendance and hospital admission data within the Patient Episode Database for Wales (equivalent to HES) in the X59 project. This will allow redistribution methods to be developed to allocate deaths coded with the X59 to other causes, principally falls, which will enable these deaths to be included in the calculation of YLL.  Fall prevention is a public health priority across the UK and accurate information on trends is needed to evaluate the impact of policy initiatives. Swansea University would like to replicate these analyses using data from England (20 times larger than Wales) to obtain greater precision using larger sample sizes, and publish the findings in a scientific journal.

Processing activities: 1. JAMIE/BRIDGE-Health:  Injury related records will be extracted from HES A&E data set only. The records will be recoded into the JAMIE Minimum Data Set format and then this coded data set will be uploaded to a restricted access EU database  (only the analysis results and no record-level data i.e. Case counts and risk/odds ratio’s and their respective confidence intervals will be present). As part of Joint Action on Monitoring Injuries in Europe (JAMIE) Swansea University submits anonymised emergency department data records to a centralised EU database. This will then enable a European Community Health Indicator (ECHI) 29b, incidence of home injuries,  to be calculated. At present, the Minimum Data Set can only be derived from the routinely collected HES Accident & Emergency dataset. The data will be made available through public access and restricted access. The public access option will assist country comparison by Incidence Rates (IR) and therefore provides access to very limited and aggregated data presentations. The restricted access option can only be used by authorised researchers. All data users have to agree (in writing) with the following terms of use:
•           Single-record data is to be used for internal purposes only. The user will not give access to single record data to a third party.  Within the SAIL gateway Swansea University will use the HES data extracts provided by HSCIC at a patient level, which is pseudonymised with ENCRYPTED_HESID being used as the patient identifier.  Only analyses results will be extracted from the secured platform, which will not be at a patient or single row data level – with a less than 5 rule employed to make sure no identifiable results can be extracted.  Outputs will contain only aggregate level data with small numbers suppressed in line with HES analysis guide.
•           Single-record data will not be published or disseminated to the public, neither to a third party;
•           The user will not link Injury Data Base (IDB) data to other information in order to identify natural persons;
•           The user may use the data only for the general purpose of research or analyses with the goal of deriving general findings to enhance safety and prevent injuries ;
•           Whenever publishing any results of such research or analyses, the user will indicate the source (“Source: EU Injury Database – The IDB Network & the EU Commission, DG SANCO”) in texts, tables, figures, and list of literature;
•           Data suppliers, network-coordinator, or data controller cannot be hold responsible for any outcome or conclusions of research and analyses; 

2. ICD10 Trauma Mortality prediction model: Regression models will be developed using data that has been linked between the HES inpatient dataset (HES APC) and the HES ONS mortality dataset, with the latter being used to indicate survival (yes/no) at 30, 93 and 365 days for comparison with different measures used around the world. Individual row level data are required to relate individual injuries to mortality, having adjusted for age, gender, other injuries and co-morbidity. More than half of injurious events result in more than one physical injury and models need to be able to account for multiple injuries.  
The dataset would contain no dates, no hospital identifiers, and no geographical data. Whilst there will inevitably be uniqueness within the large dataset individual privacy will be protected as the data cannot be removed or linked to any other source and only model parameters will be requested for removal from the SAIL Gateway. 
3. UK Burden of Falls project: For this project, processing would involve allocating deaths coded with the X59 code ('exposure to unspecified factor') to other causes by linking the HES ONS mortality data with the HES APC and HES A&E data. Those deaths allocated to falls can then be included in the calculation of Years of Life Lost to obtain a more accurate estimate of the burden of injuries from falls.

Specific outputs expected, including target date(s): 1.JAMIE/BRIDGE-Health: Outputs will involve submitting anonymised emergency department data records to a centralised EU database. This will then enable European Community Health Indicator (ECHI) 29b to be calculated. The data will be made available through public access and restricted access. The public access option will assist country comparison by Incidence Rates (IR) and therefore provides access to very limited, aggregated data presentations. The restricted access option can only be used by authorised researchers. Annual updates will be provided to EU Injury Database – The IDB Network & the EU Commission, DG SANCO (http://ec.europa.eu/health/data_collection/databases/idb/index_en.htm). Reports on injuries in Europe are made available on the following website: http://ec.europa.eu/health/data_collection/databases/idb/publications/index_en.htm
2. ICD10 Trauma Mortality Prediction Model: Outputs will include an ICD10 injury regression model which will estimate injury severities. The injury severities will be used to risk-adjust patient outcomes; this will involve developing a prediction model used to inform policy.  
Swansea University aim to publish the research in a journal such as high impact journals, Lancet, BMJ, Journal of Trauma and the Annals of Surgery.  This will be achieved by 2015/2016.
3. UK Burden of  Falls project: Outputs are expected to  include a more accurate estimate of the burden of injuries from falls since a proportion of the X59 (‘exposure to unspecified factor’) ICD10 code deaths would be attributed to falls and can therefore be included in the calculation of Years of Life Lost (YLL). Swansea University aim to publish the research in journals like Lancet, BMJ, Journal of Trauma and the Annals of Surgery. This will be achieved by 2015/2016.

Expected measurable benefits to health and/or social care, including target date(s): 1. JAMIE/BRIDGE-Health  - This data will be sent to the European Injury Database which is used to facilitate injury prevention policies and provides information on the burden of injuries (http://ec.europa.eu/health/data_collection/databases/idb/purpose_methods/index_en.htm). Annual updates will be provided to this database Incident rates and regression results will be used to inform policy.  The analysis will be done at Swansea University and sent to European Injury.  The UK population as a whole will benefit due to injury prevention policy being updated as a result of the analysis. The results of the analyses will be forwarded to the chief medical officers of the four UK countries and their lead officials and those in charge of injury prevention in Public Health England and Public Health Wales. The lead official for injury prevention in the Department of Health is Sue Maisey and in Welsh Government it is Dr Heather Payne. These individuals will review UK performance against other European countries and decide whether or not to change injury prevention policy. Injury prevention has been shown to be one of the most cost effective but under invested preventive strategies – see RoSPA Big Book on Accident Prevention for England http://www.rospa.com/RoSPAWeb/docs/public-health/big-book/index.html.  These analyses will be helpful to multiple organisations, including UK third sector organisations such as the Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents (RoSPA)and the Child Accident Prevention Trust, the four UK Departments of Health, Public Health England, Public Health Wales and their counterparts in Scotland and Northern Ireland, and also for the evaluation of NICE guidelines at a population level – see NICE Guidance – prevention of unintentional injuries in the under 15s  https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ph30
2. ICD10 Trauma Mortality Prediction Model - There are no easy to use, or affordable tools, available to measure the severity of injuries using the version of the International Classification of Diseases – version 10 (ICD 10) in operation in the UK and most of the world and soon to be introduced in the US. If an ICD10 version of the ICD9 based trauma mortality prediction model (TMPM), developed by Osler et al, could be developed it would have considerable functionality within the NHS, including facilitating:
1.         evaluation and continuous quality improvement of trauma care
2.         evaluation of the population impact of reorganization of trauma systems
3.         evaluation of preventive strategies, e.g. has the road safety strategy reduced the severity of injuries
ICD10 Trauma Mortality Prediction Model
Benefits/impact
The model and all the parameters (risk of death per ICD10 code and associated confidence intervals) will be published in a scientific journal and made available worldwide. The tool will be used by clinicians, organisations and commissioners of services to compare risk adjusted observed versus expected numbers of deaths for any service and will aid in the planning and evaluation of trauma services by the NHS across the UK. Swansea University have already achieved the same with Welsh data and wish to the same with English data.  They have the Welsh Government funded Emergency Medical Retrieval and Transfer Service will use it to evaluate the effectiveness of the service. One would expect widespread adoption of this tool across the UK, US, Canada and Australasia.  With the English data a similar method will be used in a similar way if the quality of data is good.
3. UK Burden of Falls project
The output of this research will be a model to more correctly estimate the true burden of falls that can be applied to any statistical geography to which ONS cause of mortality data are released. Currently, fall related mortality is massively underestimated.   This contributes to a lack of appropriate prioritisation for falls prevention by local health and social care providers and restrictions on their ability to measure the cost effectiveness of their services. Such a model would be widely adopted by the providers and commissioners of health and social care providers.  They have identified the issue once the analysis is carried out it will inform policy and reduce the burden of falls within the UK.
Huge numbers of older people are injured and killed following falls. However, many fall related deaths are coded to non-specific causes. This means that estimates of the population burden of falls are artificially low. Hence the importance and cost-effectiveness of prevention are undervalued and there is insufficient investment in cost-effective prevention.
The model would be expected to be used by service commissioners and to feature in updated NICE guidance – see https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg161 . That guidance also includes a research recommendation (2.2) for more UK-based cost effectiveness studies of falls prevention interventions.
The cost effectiveness of falls prevention would be increased by accurately attributing the vast majority of the 24% of UK injury deaths that are currently coded to bucket codes. The number of fall related deaths would increase very substantially as would metrics for the burden of injuries based on Disability-Adjusted Life-Years (DALYs) or Quality Adjusted Life Years (QALYs).
Public Health England basis its priorities on DALY analyses using the Global Burden of Diseases Lancet reference – 
United Kingdom performance on health: implications from the Global Burden of Diseases Study. The Lancet (published online March 5th 2013) and NICE bases its cost effectiveness metrics on QALYs. Health and social care commissioners take these appraisals into account when commissioning fall prevention services.
This will be achieved by 2015/2016.
